Indolent means habitually lazy — having a deep, settled dislike for work, effort, or activity. An indolent person is not someone who is just having a lazy Sunday or who is tired after a long week. It describes a person whose laziness is a character trait — a consistent, ongoing tendency to avoid doing things that require effort.

Think of it this way: if someone is lazy once, you might just say they're being lazy. But if someone is always avoiding work, always finding ways to do as little as possible, always choosing rest over responsibility — that person can be called indolent.
What Makes It Different from Just "Lazy"?

"Lazy" is a word everyone knows. "Indolent" means something very similar, but with a few important differences in flavour:

It's more formal and literary. You're far more likely to see "indolent" in a novel, an essay, or a formal piece of writing than in everyday conversation. If you call a friend lazy, you'd say "lazy." If a novelist is describing a character's personality with precision and style, they might write "indolent."

It implies a deeper, more ingrained quality. "Lazy" can describe a momentary state. "Indolent" almost always describes a habitual pattern — a built-in characteristic, not a one-time thing.

It carries a sense of comfortable, contented idleness. There is a subtle suggestion in "indolent" that the person is not just lazy but is comfortable being lazy — almost pleasurably so. They are not struggling to motivate themselves; they are simply unbothered by the idea of doing nothing.

So if "lazy" is a plain t-shirt, "indolent" is the same t-shirt made of fine fabric — essentially the same idea, but more refined, more precise, with a slightly richer texture.

The word carries a mildly negative judgment. When you call someone indolent, you are not being neutral — you are suggesting they lack effort, drive, or discipline. However, it is not a harsh insult. It is more of a cool, detached observation, the kind a teacher or a critic might make. It can even sound almost elegant when used to describe someone who is magnificently lazy — like a nobleman who has never worked a day in his life and sees no reason to start.

Here are several examples across different situations so you can see exactly how the word is used:

  • "He was a talented musician but far too indolent to practise regularly, and so his gift slowly faded."
    → He had the skill, but not the work ethic.
  • "The summer heat made everyone feel indolent, unwilling to move from the shade."
    → Here it describes a temporary, situational laziness brought on by the heat — a less common use, but valid.
  • "She watched her indolent colleagues scroll through their phones while deadlines passed by."
    → Describes a habitual avoidance of work.
  • "The indolent cat stretched across the entire sofa, unbothered by the world."
    → Playfully applied to an animal, it describes contented, peaceful laziness.
The Medical Meaning (Important — Don't Skip This)

"Indolent" has a completely separate and important meaning in medicine, and you will encounter it if you ever read medical texts or talk to a doctor.

In a medical context, indolent describes a disease, tumour, wound, or infection that:

  • Causes little or no pain, and/or
  • Develops or progresses very slowly

So a doctor might say, "The patient has an indolent lymphoma" — meaning it is a slow-growing cancer that is not spreading aggressively and is not causing significant pain at this stage.

Or: "The wound remained indolent, refusing to heal but causing no discomfort."

This medical meaning is completely unrelated to laziness. It is purely a technical term meaning slow, painless, inactive. The connection, if any, is loose — the disease is "sitting around doing nothing" much like an indolent person, but you must never confuse the two contexts.
Words That Are Similar (And How They Compare)

• Lazy — the everyday, informal equivalent. Broader and less precise.
  • Slothful — even stronger than indolent; implies a moral failing, almost a sin-level of laziness.
  • Idle — simply means not working or not active; it is more neutral and does not judge character the way "indolent" does.
  • Lethargic — refers more to a physical sluggishness, often due to illness, tiredness, or low energy. You can be lethargic without being lazy by nature.
  • Apathetic — means not caring or feeling no interest; it is about emotion and motivation, not specifically about avoiding work.

Among these, indolent is best used when you want to describe a person's habitual, characteristic avoidance of effort, in a formal or literary tone.

If indolent is one end of the spectrum, the other end includes words like:

  • Diligent — careful, steady, and hardworking
  • Industrious — consistently active and productive
  • Assiduous — showing great care and persistent effort
  • Energetic — full of active enthusiasm and drive

Use indolent when:

  • You are writing formally or literarily.
  • You want to describe a person's habitual laziness as a characteristic trait.
  • You are reading or writing in a medical context (slow-growing, painless).

Avoid using it in casual conversation — it will sound unnatural. In speech, "lazy" almost always works better. Save "indolent" for writing where precision and a slightly elevated tone are appropriate.

Indolent means habitually, characteristically lazy — a settled, comfortable avoidance of work and effort. In medicine, it means slow-moving and causing little pain. In all cases, it is a formal, precise, and slightly literary word.
